posts:
Tokenization gets pitched as something coming for Treasuries, gold and real estate.

By the only metric that counts — value actually moved on-chain — it already happened. Years ago.

The asset that won was the dollar.

A stablecoin IS tokenization: a token issued against a reserve of dollars held off-chain, redeemable against that reserve, transferable on a public blockchain.

That's the same structure as tokenized gold or a tokenized Treasury fund. Not a metaphor. The literal shape.

So stablecoins aren't a preview of real-world-asset tokenization.

They're its largest result to date.

>$300B in stablecoins circulate on-chain, against roughly $32–48B for every OTHER tokenized real-world asset combined.

The numbers nobody puts side by side:

CoinDesk Data, July 2026 — stablecoins ~$308B vs $32.1B for non-stablecoin tokenized RWAs. That second figure was the highest it had ever been.

Token Terminal, same quarter: ~$346B total on-chain tokenized value, stablecoins ~86% of it.

The remainder — led by tokenized Treasuries at ~$15B — split across every other category.

Figures differ by tracker and by week, because trackers include different token sets and measure distributed vs represented value differently.

We're not going to pretend to a precision that doesn't exist. But every major source lands in the same place.

And the rest of tokenization is NOT standing still.

CoinGecko: RWAs excluding stablecoins grew 256.7% in fifteen months — $5.42B (Jan 2025) to $19.32B (end of Q1 2026).

That's a real growth rate.

It's also, on CoinGecko's own framing, still only ~6.4% the size of the stablecoin market — up from 2.7% a year earlier.

Fast growth off a small base. Both halves of that sentence matter.

Why did stablecoins win first? Not an accident of timing. A structural head start.

Demand for dollars is already universal. A stablecoin doesn't have to CREATE a market — only move an existing one onto a faster rail.

Tokenized Treasuries and gold carry friction before they can even compete.

Most are gated to accredited or institutional buyers. Most route through a transfer-agent or allowlist layer deciding who may hold the token at all.

A token that reverts if it lands in the wrong wallet is solving a compliance problem before it can solve a convenience problem.

A dollar stablecoin, for most of its users, has no such gate.

There's a simpler reason too.

Most people who want gold or Treasury exposure can already get it in a brokerage account in a few taps. Tokenization has to beat an incumbent that's already easy.

Cross-border dollar access is the opposite case.

Now what "winning" does NOT mean, because this is where the analogy stops.

Holding a stablecoin means holding a claim on an issuer's promise to redeem, backed by a reserve that issuer controls and reports on.

That claim is only as good as the reserve, the audits behind it, and the issuer's solvency.

The identical counterparty question that applies to a tokenized Treasury fund or a tokenized gold bar.

Tokenization moved the asset onto a faster, more transferable rail.

It did not remove the issuer sitting in the middle of the claim. And it did not make every stablecoin interchangeable — reserve composition, audit cadence and jurisdiction all differ.

To be explicit: this is a market-structure observation about tokenization broadly, not a claim about any stablecoin Swop issues.

Swop doesn't issue one.

Where we sit: Swop is fully self-custodial — keys are generated and held on your device; Swop never holds them.

It runs on Solana, Ethereum, Base and Polygon, and transactions are gas-sponsored, so moving a stablecoin doesn't mean first buying a second asset for gas.

What the next wave borrows from stablecoins is the part that mattered: an asset you can hold yourself, move without permission, and settle instantly.

Rather than one merely described on a blockchain while the real custody arrangement stays exactly as it was.
